title: Hiring a Contractor in Broward County: 12 Questions to Ask
imageAlt: Residential driveway and exterior by Oak Park Construction
content:
Hiring a contractor here is not the same as hiring one anywhere else. Broward sits inside a
hurricane-zone code that most of the country never deals with, permitting runs through your individual
city rather than one county office, and flood zone can quietly reshape a project before it starts.

Most homeowners know they should ask questions. Fewer know which ones matter *here*. These twelve do.

## Licence, insurance, and whether they can legally do the work

### 1. Does your Florida license cover this work?

Ask for the license number, type and business name, then check the current record yourself through
Florida [DBPR's license search](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp). Make sure the license
class fits the proposed work and the proposal names the business you are hiring. Oak Park Construction
is listed under Matthew McFolling's active **Certified Building Contractor** license, CBC1263425;
[DBPR's record](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/LicenseDetail.asp?SID=&id=BD9747F01F094DD9A193F8D24BF3A91B)
shows the Oak Park Construction DBA. Check it again before signing because status can change.

If a bidder will not give you a license number or the record does not match, pause the hiring decision
and resolve that discrepancy before paying a deposit.

### 2. Do you carry general liability insurance and workers' compensation?

Ask for a certificate of insurance, not a verbal yes. Check that the policy is current and that the
coverage is sized for your project.

Then ask the follow-up most people miss: **do your subcontractors carry their own?** Most contractors
use subs. Ask your insurer or adviser what coverage and documentation are appropriate for your project; do not infer coverage from a verbal answer.

### 3. Will you pull all the required permits yourself?

Permitting in Broward runs through individual cities, not one county office. Pompano Beach, Fort
Lauderdale and Hollywood each have their own submittal requirements and their own review times. Your
contractor should know your city's process and handle it start to finish.

Ask the building department which permits the exact scope requires and who will apply for them. If a
bidder proposes owner-pulled permits, ask the department what responsibilities that creates before
accepting the arrangement. Keep permit and final-inspection records with your house documents.

## Scope, timeline and money

### 4. What exactly is in this contract, and what isn't?

This is where homeowners get hurt most often. A low bid means nothing if the scope is vague.

Have them walk you through every line. Is demolition included? Debris removal? Permit fees?
Inspections? Final cleanup? Then look hard at **allowances** — the placeholder amounts for tile,
fixtures and cabinetry. Allowances are where a reasonable-looking contract quietly becomes an expensive
one. Ask what the allowance actually buys, and ask to see something at that price.

### 5. What is a realistic timeline, and what could move it?

Weather, material lead times and permit review can move exterior work. Ask which dates in the proposed
schedule depend on approvals, deliveries or inspections.

A good contractor gives you a range and names the risks. Ask what has actually delayed their recent
projects. That answer tells you more about their experience than anything on their website.

### 6. How do you handle change orders?

Something unexpected turns up on nearly every project that touches an existing building. What matters
is what happens next.

Ask directly: *will I get a written change order, with a price and a schedule impact, before any extra
work starts?* If the answer is anything other than yes, keep looking.

### 7. What is the payment schedule?

Payments should track progress — deposit, then milestones like foundation complete, framing inspected,
rough-ins done, final walkthrough. That structure protects both sides.

A reasonable deposit is normal. A large lump sum before anyone mobilises is not.

## Structure, code, and the things specific to South Florida

### 8. How does the Florida Building Code affect this specific project?

Broward is in the Florida Building Code's High Velocity Hurricane Zone. The project designer and
local building department determine the applicable wind requirements, opening protection and structural
connections for the specific work. Ask how those requirements appear in the drawings and bid.

Ask them to explain, in plain language, how that shapes *your* project. A contractor who has built here
can do that without notes. One who cannot has probably not built here long.

### 9. Is this property in a flood zone, and what does that change?

Flood information can affect the design and approvals for certain work. Search the address first, then
ask the designer and building department whether elevation information or other flood-related
requirements apply to your proposal.

Ask whether you need a survey or an elevation certificate before design starts — not after. Broward
publishes [flood information by property](https://www.broward.org/ENVIRONMENT),
and FEMA's [flood map service centre](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search) shows the mapped zone.

### 10. Who is actually on site every day?

Ask who runs your job day to day, how often they are there, and who you call when something is wrong.
"The owner will be involved" is not an answer. A name is.

### 11. Can I see work you finished, and talk to those owners?

Photos prove a job existed. A conversation proves how it went. Ask for owners from projects of a
similar type and size, and ask them one specific question: *what happened when something went wrong?*

### 12. What does the end look like?

Ask how a project closes: the punch list, the final inspection, what warranty covers, for how long, and
who to call in eighteen months. A contractor who has thought about the end has usually thought about
the middle too.

## What good answers sound like

You are not testing anyone's memory. You are listening for whether they have done this here, recently,
and whether they will put things in writing.

Vagueness on scope, reluctance about permits, pressure for a large deposit, or hand-waving about
hurricane code — any of those is worth more attention than the price on the last page.

If you are working through this on a specific project, we handle [additions](/services/additions),
[full renovations](/services/full-renovation), [kitchens](/services/kitchen),
[bathrooms](/services/bathroom) and [new construction](/services/new-construction) across Broward. You
can see finished South Florida work in our [portfolio](/portfolio).

Bring these twelve questions to whoever you are considering — including us.

title: What Actually Drives the Cost of a Home Addition in Broward County
imageAlt: Oak Park Construction home addition in progress
content:
A useful addition budget starts with a decision: what new space must the house provide, and what work will that require in this particular building? A price per square foot cannot answer whether the existing structure can support the plan, where utilities will connect, or what the local permit office will require. Use the steps below to get comparable proposals before choosing a contractor.

## Start with a one-page scope, not a price target

Write down the room's intended use, approximate size, and whether it needs a bathroom, kitchen, laundry, or separate entrance. Mark the wall where you expect it to join the house. List the finishes you care about and the ones you could simplify. Then give the same brief to every designer or contractor you consult.

Before asking for a firm construction price, gather what you already have: a survey, any plans for the existing house, known permit records, and photos of the proposed tie-in. If a document is missing, ask who will obtain it and whether that work is included in the proposal. A site visit can reveal questions; it cannot replace a structural evaluation where one is needed.

**Decision point:** If your real problem is a poor layout rather than insufficient area, price a [full renovation](/services/full-renovation) alongside the addition. If you need a new bedroom or living area that cannot fit inside the present footprint, continue with the addition study.

## Check the constraints that can change the design

**Property and zoning.** Ask the permitting office for your address about setbacks, lot coverage, easements, and any local review that applies before assuming the addition will fit where you drew it. Broward's [Building Code Division](https://www.broward.org/BUILDING) handles permitting in the Broward Municipal Services District; municipalities have their own processes. Confirm the authority for your address instead of using a neighbor's permit estimate.

**Flood information.** Look up the address in FEMA's [Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search). A map is a starting point, not an elevation determination for your design. Ask the designer and local building department whether a survey, elevation information, or flood-related requirements affect the proposed floor level and foundation. Resolve that question before pricing the foundation as a simple slab.

**Wind and the connection to the house.** Broward is within the Florida Building Code's High Velocity Hurricane Zone. The structural designer must account for the applicable wind requirements, openings, and the connection from the new roof through the walls into the foundation. Ask each bidder whether their price includes engineering, approved opening products, and the work at the roof and wall tie-in. A quote that omits those items is not comparable to one that includes them.

**Existing systems.** A bathroom or kitchen addition needs more than fixtures: locate the drainage route, water supply, electrical capacity, and air-conditioning connection. Ask what has been checked and what is still an allowance or assumption. If a wall will be removed, ask whether temporary support and the final beam are included.

## Compare bids by scope, not by the last number

Give each bidder the same plans and scope revision. Put the proposals side by side and mark each of these items as included, excluded, or unresolved:

- Design, engineering, survey, permit applications, plan review, and fees.
- Site preparation, demolition, disposal, foundation, structure, roof tie-in, and weather protection during construction.
- Windows and doors, electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling, insulation, drywall, and finishes.
- Utility upgrades, work needed in the existing rooms, landscaping or paving repair, and final inspections.
- Allowances for selections, with the amount and the product or quality level each allowance buys.
- The schedule assumptions, payment milestones, warranty terms, and the written change-order process.

If one price is lower, ask the bidder to identify the exact scope difference in writing. A missing panel upgrade or roof tie-in may be more important than a lower finish allowance. Do not treat an allowance as a fixed price; compare what each allowance actually covers. Keep a separate contingency for discoveries in the existing house, and ask how a discovery is documented and approved before extra work begins.

## Choose the next step for your stage

**Still deciding whether to add on?** Pay for the feasibility questions first: location on the lot, possible tie-in, structural constraints, utilities, and permit authority. That work can prevent you from commissioning a design that cannot be priced or approved as imagined.

**Already have plans?** Ask for proposals against the same plan set and selection list. Request a list of exclusions and unresolved assumptions with every bid. Ask which changes would require revised plans or a new permit review.

**Ready to select a contractor?** Verify the contractor's license through Florida [DBPR's license search](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp), request current insurance documentation, and agree on who applies for permits and schedules inspections. Confirm the license and business name on the proposal match the records you check.

An addition is worth pursuing when it solves a space problem the existing floor plan cannot solve and the property can support the work. If you are comparing those options for a Broward home, bring your address, survey if available, and a one-page scope to the first conversation. Ask for the design and site questions to be identified before anyone promises a construction figure. Our [additions team](/services/additions) can help scope that first step; you can review our [completed work](/portfolio) before deciding whom to call.

title: Shell Construction in South Florida: What It Is and Why It's Different
content:
If you are planning a new build or a large addition, "shell" is the word that will come up first and
get explained least.

A shell is the structural skeleton of the building — foundation, exterior walls, roof structure, and
usually the exterior openings. It stops before interior finishes. The words “dry shell” and “cold dark shell” can describe different delivery conditions. Ask for a
written inclusion list instead of relying on the label.

It is also the phase where mistakes are most expensive, because everything after it is built on top of
what you did here. You can change a countertop later. You cannot easily change a slab.

## What a shell typically includes

Scope varies by contract, but a South Florida shell usually covers:

- **Site prep and grading** — clearing, levelling, and getting the lot ready for the pour
- **Foundation** — the engineered system specified for that site and design
- **Structural walls** — concrete block or another system specified by the engineer
- **Roof framing and sheathing** — the designed roof structure and deck
- **Exterior windows and doors** — impact-rated or protected, per the calculated loads for each opening
- **Dry-in or final roofing** — depending on what the contract says
- **Rough sleeves** — electrical conduit and plumbing penetrations set during the slab and block phase

**What a shell excludes matters just as much:** interior framing, drywall, insulation, HVAC ductwork,
finish plumbing and electrical, flooring, paint. That is the build-out, and it is a separate phase.

Some owners hire one contractor for the shell and another for the interior. It can work. It also means
two contracts, two schedules, and a seam where responsibility can get blurry — particularly if
something in the shell needs adjusting once interior trades start. One coordinated contract can simplify that boundary, but the responsibilities still need to be written down.

## Why South Florida makes this harder

Building a shell is technical anywhere. Three things make it genuinely different here.

### Hurricane-zone code

Broward is inside the Florida Building Code's **High Velocity Hurricane Zone**. Its design and
product requirements have to be resolved for the actual building, not inferred from a generic shell price.

In practice that means a continuous load path — from the anchor bolts in the foundation, up through the
block and tie beam, to the roof-to-wall connections — with specified hardware, specified quantities, and
inspections that check them. Exterior openings must be impact-rated or protected by approved shutters,
with product approvals matched to the pressures calculated for each opening.

Ask which drawings and approved products will be submitted and how the contractor coordinates with
the engineer before construction begins.

### Soil and the water table

Soil, groundwater and drainage conditions vary by lot. Ask what site information the foundation
designer needs and which assumptions are still open. The drawings should define the foundation,
waterproofing or moisture details and grading required for this project.

### An inspection sequence you cannot shortcut

The inspections required depend on the jurisdiction and scope. Ask the building department and
contractor which stages must be inspected before they are covered, who schedules them, and how an
inspection delay affects subsequent work. Put those dependencies in the schedule rather than assuming
every stage can start on a fixed date.

## Residential and commercial shells are not the same job

**Residential** — a single-family home or an addition in Weston, Miramar or Parkland typically means
slab, CBS block walls, trusses, sheathing, impact openings and exterior doors. If you are adding a
second storey or a new room, the shell phase also has to tie new structure into the existing building.
That tie-in is engineering, and it is the part that most often changes after the survey.

**Commercial** — retail, office, restaurant or medical shells bring larger open spans, often steel
structural elements, and different fire-rating requirements. A landlord frequently delivers a cold dark
shell and the tenant builds out from there, which makes the boundary between the two scopes a contract
question as much as a construction one.

## Where shells actually go wrong

These are scope and coordination problems worth testing before work starts:

- **The shell contractor and the engineer are not talking.** Drawings say one thing, the pour happens
  another way, and it is discovered at inspection.
- **Sleeves in the wrong place.** Conduit and plumbing penetrations set during the slab and block phase
  are very hard to move afterwards. This is a coordination failure, not a skill failure.
- **The tie-in was priced before anyone looked.** On additions especially, what the existing structure
  can carry is not knowable from the street.
- **The scope boundary was vague.** "Shell" without a written inclusion list is how two contractors each
  assume the other is doing the dry-in.
- **Dry-in timing was vague.** Ask who protects exposed work if weather interrupts the sequence.

A written responsibility list gives the owner and both contractors a way to resolve these questions before work is covered.

## Getting it right

Ask for the inclusion list in writing before anything is priced. Ask who coordinates with the engineer.
Ask what the inspection sequence is and who books it. And check the license type and status through Florida's
[DBPR license search](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp). Oak Park Construction's Certified Building Contractor license is CBC1263425.

We build [shells and structural work](/services/shell-construction), the
[concrete and slab work](/services/concrete-pavers) underneath them, and
[new construction](/services/new-construction) and [additions](/services/additions) from shell through
finish under one contract. Completed South Florida work is in our [portfolio](/portfolio).

## If you have plans

Send us the drawings and the address. We can review the proposed scope, identify information still needed from the designer and permit
office, and clarify what a shell bid includes before you compare prices.

title: Planning a Fort Lauderdale Home Renovation: Scope Before Selections
imageAlt: Finished OPC kitchen renovation; illustrative of renovation planning
author: Oak Park Construction
content:
A renovation gets easier to price when everyone is describing the same work. “Update the kitchen” might mean cabinets and finishes, or it might mean moving plumbing, opening a wall, changing electrical service, and rebuilding the room around a new layout. Those are different projects. Before asking for bids, decide which problem the renovation must solve and what you are willing to change to solve it.

## Separate the desired result from the proposed work

Write a short brief in two columns. In the first, name the outcome: more storage, a safer bathroom, a kitchen that works for two cooks, or a floor plan that admits more daylight. In the second, list the work you think it requires. Keep them separate because a contractor or designer may find a simpler way to meet the outcome.

Then mark each room as **cosmetic**, **systems**, or **structural**. Repainting and replacing cabinets in the same layout differ from moving drains, adding circuits, or removing a wall. Ask which work needs drawings, engineering, permit review, and inspections. Fort Lauderdale's [Development Services guidance](https://www.fortlauderdale.gov/Government/Departments/Development-Services/HB-803) shows why even apparently small work has project-specific exceptions; get an answer for your address and scope rather than assuming a category is exempt.

If the home is outside Fort Lauderdale, confirm the correct municipal building department. [Broward County's Building Code Division](https://www.broward.org/BUILDING) serves the Broward Municipal Services District and certain regional functions; it is not the permit counter for every city address.

## Resolve the expensive unknowns before comparing bids

Gather your survey, any existing plans, permit records, and photos of the affected rooms. Ask the contractor to identify what cannot be confirmed until a wall or floor is opened. That list is part of a useful proposal, not an admission of uncertainty to hide.

For a bathroom or kitchen, ask where new water and drain lines would run and whether the electrical panel has room for the proposed load. For an open-plan change, ask who determines whether a wall is load-bearing and designs the support if needed. For work at exterior openings or the roof, ask how the proposed products and connections will be checked against current requirements. In Broward's High Velocity Hurricane Zone, those questions can change the scope before finishes are chosen.

If the property may be in a flood hazard area, check its address through FEMA's [Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search), then ask the designer and permitting office what information is needed for this particular alteration. The map alone does not settle the design.

## Make proposals comparable

Give every bidder the same brief and plan revision. Ask each to state what is included, excluded, and still an allowance. Compare these items line by line:

- Demolition, disposal, temporary protection, and repair to adjoining rooms.
- Design and engineering, permit submission, fees, and inspection coordination.
- Electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling, and any system upgrades.
- Cabinets, tile, fixtures, flooring, paint, and the exact selections behind allowances.
- Work hours, access, dust separation, and whether the family can use the home during each phase.
- Payment milestones, schedule assumptions, warranty, and written change-order process.

A lower total may reflect a smaller scope or a different allowance. Ask the bidder to explain differences in writing before choosing. Keep a contingency for conditions that cannot be seen until demolition; agree on how proposed extra work will be priced and approved before it starts.

## Decide whether to renovate, add space, or stage the work

If the existing footprint can meet the goal, a [full renovation](/services/full-renovation) may avoid the additional property and structural questions of an addition. If the goal requires new floor area, review our [addition planning guide](/how-much-does-a-home-addition-cost-in-broward-county) and compare both options against the same household need. If budget or disruption is the constraint, ask whether the work can be split into phases without paying twice for demolition or reopening finished walls.

Before signing, verify the contractor's license through Florida [DBPR's search](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp), request current insurance documentation, and confirm who will apply for permits and schedule inspections. A useful first meeting should leave you with a clearer scope and a list of unresolved conditions. Bring that list, your address, and any plans when you talk with our [renovation team](/services/full-renovation); our [portfolio](/portfolio) shows the kind of project work we undertake.

title: Drywall During a South Florida Renovation: What to Decide First
imageAlt: Finished OPC bathroom; illustrative of interior finish planning
author: Oak Park Construction
content:
Drywall is usually discussed near the end of a renovation, when everyone is thinking about paint. The decisions that determine the result come earlier: whether a wall is dry and sound, what work must be inspected behind it, and how smooth the finished surface needs to be. If those questions are answered after the boards go up, correcting them means opening finished work.

## First decide whether the wall is ready to close

Before replacing board, identify why the old surface failed. A stain can come from a roof leak, plumbing, air-conditioning condensation, or water entering at an opening. Covering the stain without finding the source leaves the problem behind the new finish. The [EPA's moisture guidance](https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home) puts moisture control at the center of mold prevention; damaged materials and hidden cavities need assessment and drying before enclosure.

Ask what will be checked while the wall is open: the substrate, any visible moisture damage, insulation, and the plumbing or electrical work in the cavity. If a permitted trade or structural change is part of the project, ask the local building department or contractor which inspection must happen before closure. Permit requirements differ by scope and jurisdiction. Fort Lauderdale's [current guidance](https://www.fortlauderdale.gov/Government/Departments/Development-Services/HB-803) distinguishes possible minor interior work from structural and utility changes; it does not make every drywall job permit-free.

## Specify the finish you expect to see

“Ready for paint” is not a precise finish specification. The [Gypsum Association's GA-214 guidance](https://gypsum.org/2022/02/revised-levels-of-finish-for-gypsum-panel-products-released/) describes levels of finish so designers and contractors can choose an appearance appropriate to the final decoration and lighting. Ask which level is included in the proposal, and view a sample where possible. Bright side light, dark paint, and glossy finishes reveal surface variation more readily than a utility-room finish.

A useful scope names the rooms, finish level, corner treatment, texture if any, primer, and how existing surfaces will meet new ones. If only one part of a room is repaired, ask whether the price includes blending the patch across the visible plane. A perfectly finished patch can still stand out when the surrounding wall has a different texture.

## Plan for dust, moisture, and people living in the home

Sanding and demolition affect adjacent rooms. Ask how the work area will be separated, how supply and return vents will be protected, where debris will go, and who cleans before primer. Ask how indoor moisture will be controlled while compound dries and before paint is applied. A schedule should allow the materials to dry under the actual site conditions rather than promising a fixed number of days for every house.

If a bathroom or other wet area is involved, ask the designer or contractor which board, backing, waterproofing system, and finish belong in each location. Board color alone is not a waterproofing plan. Request the product and installation details for the assembly, especially around tubs, showers, and penetrations.

## Choose a small repair or a larger renovation scope

A sound, dry wall with a small isolated hole may only need a local patch. Repeated staining, soft material, a wall that must be opened for trades, or a room-wide finish change calls for a broader assessment. This distinction protects you from paying for a beautiful surface over an unresolved cause.

When drywall is part of a [bathroom](/services/bathroom), [kitchen](/services/kitchen), or [full renovation](/services/full-renovation), ask for the opening, inspection, closure, finish, and cleanup sequence in one scope. Bring photos showing both the damaged area and the wider room to the first conversation. Our [project gallery](/portfolio) can help you decide whether the work you are considering is a small repair or part of a complete renovation; Oak Park Construction takes on the latter as part of full projects.

title: A Broward Home Flip: Decide the Renovation Scope Before the Purchase
imageAlt: OPC renovation in progress; illustrative of renovation scope
author: Oak Park Construction
content:
A flip can look straightforward in photographs: replace finishes, improve the layout, and put the home back on the market. The purchase decision depends on what the photographs cannot show. Before assuming the work is cosmetic, identify the building and permit questions that could change the scope. This is a construction checklist, not a projection of resale price or profit.

## Make the first visit a fact-finding visit

Take a record of the roof, exterior openings, visible cracks or water staining, electrical panel, plumbing fixtures, air-conditioning equipment, and any rooms that appear to have been altered. Photograph the proposed changes and list what remains unknown. A visual visit cannot certify concealed conditions or replace an engineer's or specialist's assessment where one is needed.

Ask for the seller's available plans, survey, and permit history. For an address in the Broward Municipal Services District, the county provides a [permit search by address](https://dpepp.broward.org/BCS/Default.aspx?PossePresentation=ParcelSearchByAddress). For a city property, use that city's building department and records. Compare what was built with what the records show; ask the permitting office how any discrepancy would affect the proposed work.

Check the address in FEMA's [Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search). If the proposed renovation may alter the building substantially, ask the designer and building department whether flood-related rules or elevation information change the plan. Do this before committing to a layout or construction allowance.

## Separate the work into three scopes

**Required building work:** conditions that must be investigated or corrected to deliver the proposed project safely and obtain the necessary approvals. This may include concealed damage, structural design, utilities, or exterior openings. Do not put an unverified item in this column as if the repair is certain; mark it for investigation.

**Functional improvements:** changes that make the home work better, such as a different kitchen plan, a usable bathroom, or better circulation. Ask whether each change needs another trade or a structural alteration.

**Finish choices:** flooring, cabinetry, tile, paint, lighting, and hardware. These are visible in listing photos, but they are the easiest choices to defer until the first two scopes are understood.

Give every bidder the same three-part list. Request separate assumptions and allowances for work that cannot be confirmed before demolition. A proposal should also say who obtains drawings, applies for permits, schedules inspections, and documents changes.

## Put time in the right order

A practical sequence is investigation, design, permit review where required, demolition and discovery, structural or trade work, required inspections, enclosure, finishes, final inspections, and sale preparation. Some activities overlap, but finish work cannot erase a missing inspection or resolve a design question after the wall is closed.

Ask what can be done before closing on the property, what requires access or seller permission, and which assumptions could delay the start. Do not build a purchase decision on a fixed permit turnaround quoted for another municipality. Broward's [Building Code Division](https://www.broward.org/BUILDING) serves the unincorporated district; cities administer their own building permits.

## Decide whether the project fits your capacity

Before making an offer, write down the largest unresolved construction questions and how you will get answers. If the needed work may include a roof, panel, major plumbing, and a changed floor plan, treat it as a [full renovation](/services/full-renovation), not a cosmetic refresh. If the plan adds floor area, read the [addition scope guide](/how-much-does-a-home-addition-cost-in-broward-county) and test that separate decision.

Verify any contractor you may hire through Florida [DBPR's license search](https://www.myfloridalicense.com/wl11.asp). Request a scope that states what is included, excluded, and still contingent on investigation. If you are weighing a Broward property, bring the address, survey and permit records if available, and the changes you hope to make. Our [portfolio](/portfolio) shows completed and in-progress OPC work; a first construction conversation should help you identify the questions to resolve before you commit to the renovation.
